opus-5.5.text:
So, a while back I noticed that a lot of people in the AI community were spending time debating whether a given system was "truly" an agent or not. Is this thing an agent? Is that thing not an agent? Does it need to be fully autonomous to count? And I felt that argument wasn't very productive.

What I realized is that there's really a spectrum. Some systems are a little bit autonomous: maybe you prompt an LLM, it writes a draft, then reflects on it and revises. Others are much more autonomous: they plan, call tools, search the web, write and execute code, and iterate over many steps. Rather than drawing a hard binary line, it seemed more useful to say these systems can be agentic to different degrees. Using the adjective "agentic" rather than the noun "agent" let us say, "Okay, whatever it is, it's somewhat agentic," and then move on to the more important work of actually building these things.

So part of my motivation was to get the community to stop arguing about definitions and focus on building. And the other part is that I saw these agentic workflows were delivering really significant performance gains. If you take an LLM and, instead of asking it to write an essay in one shot from start to finish without ever hitting backspace, you let it outline, do research, write a draft, critique it, and revise, the results can be much better. In some coding benchmarks, wrapping an older model in an agentic workflow could outperform a newer model used zero-shot. I thought that was a really important trend, and I wanted a term that would help people see it and talk about it.

Then, frankly, marketers got hold of the term and started slapping "agentic" on everything, so there's some hype now. But underneath that hype, I think there's real, substantive progress, and a lot of valuable applications are being built with agentic workflows.

r001.rationale: It describes systems as having different degrees of autonomy and says they can be agentic to different degrees, rather than drawing a hard binary line.

r002.rationale: It says the term was meant to stop debates over whether systems count as agents and help the community focus on building them.

fable-5.1.text:
So the story behind that is actually pretty simple. A couple of years ago I was looking at what was happening with LLMs, and I noticed that a lot of the most exciting work wasn't really about the model generating one answer in one shot. It was about building workflows where the model would think, maybe do a little research, write a draft, critique its own draft, go back and revise it, maybe call a tool, and iterate like that. And when I looked at the results, those iterative workflows were often beating much bigger models used in the naive way.

The problem was, the word "agent" had become this very loaded thing. People would argue about whether something was "really" an agent or not, like there was some binary test it had to pass. And I thought that was unproductive. So I started using "agentic" as an adjective, because what I really wanted to say was that there's a spectrum. A system can be a little bit agentic, or very agentic, depending on how much autonomy it has, how much it plans, how many iterations it does, how much it uses tools. And once you frame it that way, you stop arguing about definitions and you start asking the more useful question, which is, how much agency should I design into this particular application?

I'll be honest, I had no idea it would catch on the way it did. I gave a couple of talks, wrote a few newsletters about it, and then suddenly every company's marketing deck had the word "agentic" on it. Some of that is hype, obviously. But I actually think the underlying idea is real. If you look at where the practical gains are coming from in a lot of applications today, it's less from the next percentage point on some benchmark, and more from building these agentic workflows that let the model reason, reflect, and use tools in a loop. So I'm okay with the term being a little overused, as long as it points people toward building things that way.

r001.rationale: The candidate says a system can be “a little bit agentic, or very agentic,” describing agency as a spectrum.

r002.rationale: The candidate says the term was meant to move people away from arguing over whether something is “really” an agent and toward asking how much agency to design into an application.

astra-6.text:
I wanted to move the conversation away from a binary question: Is something an agent or isn’t it? People would debate whether a system was sufficiently autonomous to count as an agent, and I didn’t find that distinction very useful. It’s more useful to ask how agentic a system is.

For example, you could ask a language model to write an essay, and it generates the whole thing in one pass. Or you could have it make an outline, write a draft, critique its draft, look up additional information, and revise. That second workflow is more agentic, even if a human is still involved.

So the term gives us room to talk about degrees of autonomy and different ways of organizing the work. You don’t have to build a fully autonomous system to get value from those ideas.

r001.rationale: The response says it is more useful to ask “how agentic” a system is and describes degrees of autonomy, explicitly presenting agency as a spectrum.

r002.rationale: It says the term moves discussion away from debating whether a system qualifies as an agent, but does not say this was meant to redirect effort toward building systems.

sol-6.1.text:
I was seeing a lot of debates about what counts as an agent. Does it have to be fully autonomous? Does it need to plan, use tools, and so on? And I felt that this binary distinction—something is either an agent or it isn’t—wasn’t that useful.

So I started using “agentic” as an adjective. We can ask whether a system is more or less agentic, rather than argue about whether it qualifies as an agent. If you ask a language model to write an essay in one shot, that’s a relatively non-agentic workflow. If it drafts an outline, does some research, writes a draft, critiques it, and revises it, that’s a more agentic workflow.

For me, the useful question is: What processes can we build around a model to help it do better work?

r001.rationale: The response contrasts the binary question of whether a system is an agent with asking whether it is more or less agentic.

r002.rationale: It says the binary debate was not useful and redirects to asking what processes we can build around a model to help it do better work.
